title: "K-pop Has Left Korea Behind" — The Uncomfortable Truth Behind 60% Overseas Revenue
excerpt: Stray Kids hit No. 2 on the IFPI Global Artist Chart while idol music's share of Korean streaming dropped from 21.7% to 14.1%. Album exports hit a record $301.7M, but domestic sales fell for the second straight year. K-pop is conquering the world — and quietly losing its home crowd in the process.
author: MEARROW Editorial Desk
content:
In 2025, Stray Kids ranked No. 2 on the IFPI Global Artist Chart. Seventeen landed at No. 14. One K-pop group set an unprecedented record of eight consecutive albums debuting at No. 1 on the Billboard 200. By the numbers, K-pop has never been bigger.

So why is it shrinking at home?

Idol music's share of the Circle Chart's top 400 tracks fell from 21.7% in 2024 to 14.1% in 2025. Dance tracks in Melon's top 100 slipped from 45 to 38. K-pop album exports grew 3.4% year-over-year to a record $301.7 million — but total domestic album sales dropped 7.5%, marking the second consecutive annual decline.

The world's most exported music genre is losing its domestic audience. That's not a paradox. It's a strategy — and it's starting to show its costs.

## The Revenue Map Has Already Shifted

Look at where the money actually comes from. From January to September 2025, overseas revenue accounted for 59% of HYBE's total, 60% of JYP's, and 51% of YG's. Even SM, historically the most domestically anchored of the Big Four, pulled 35% of its revenue from abroad.

For the agencies, this makes complete financial sense. Overseas fans spend more on merchandise, pay higher concert ticket prices, and represent markets that Korean fans simply can't match in scale. The pivot to global isn't irrational — it's arithmetic.

But arithmetic doesn't capture everything. As agencies optimize for international audiences, the relationship with domestic fans is quietly being renegotiated. Music critic Lim Hee-yoon puts it plainly: storytelling has become more integral than songs in idol promotions. The music is almost secondary to the mythology built around it — a mythology designed to travel across language barriers, not to resonate in a specific cultural context.

Circle Chart journalist Kim Jin-woo frames the domestic side of this equation bluntly: "domestic listeners' exhaustion with K-pop's increasingly global-oriented strategy, shown in a noticeable increase in English lyrics."

![K-pop Global Revenue vs. Domestic Revenue — Overseas Revenue Dependency by Agency](/images/news/kpop-korean-market-optional-global-paradox-1.webp)
_With overseas revenue shares crossing 50% at most major agencies, Korea's slice of the pie keeps shrinking_

## Global Hits, Domestic Disconnect

The 2025 IFPI data confirmed what many already suspected: Rosé's 'APT.' and K-pop Demon Hunters scored among the biggest global hits of the year. Both broke internationally before — and bigger than — they did at home.

This is the new K-pop playbook. The old model was: prove yourself in Korea, then export. The new model is: design for global from day one, and treat Korea as a launch platform rather than a proving ground.

Two industry insiders have pushed back on this shift, and their objections are worth taking seriously. Beat Interactive CEO Kim Hye-im said: "K-pop is rooted here. Something Korean that's not really popular in Korea being popular in the United States feels unnatural." Singing Beetle CEO Michelle Cho echoed the concern from a different angle: "K-pop started in Korea, and having something like a certification mark at home certainly helps when promoting overseas."

Neither of these is a nostalgic argument. Both are practical ones. The "made in Korea" identity isn't just cultural pride — it's a marketing asset. When domestic audiences stop caring, that asset starts to depreciate.

## The Trainee Pipeline Is Being Rebuilt for Export

This shift doesn't stop at the stage. It reaches back to the very beginning of the K-pop production chain: trainee selection.

A decade ago, agencies scouted for domestic charm — variety show charisma, the ability to connect with Korean fans, an instinct for local pop culture. Today, the checklist looks different. English fluency, global social media presence, and the capacity to build parasocial relationships across language barriers have moved to the top. Language training comes before variety skills. Global appeal is screened for before domestic relatability.

The groups debuting now are increasingly engineered to minimize friction for international fans rather than to maximize resonance with Korean ones. Short-term, this works. The revenue numbers prove it. But as the gap between K-pop and its home audience widens, something harder to quantify is being lost.

## What Happens When the Origin Story Loses Its Audience

K-pop's global appeal has always been partly built on the mystique of its origin. The rigorous training system, the performance precision, the intricate fan culture — all of it carries the implicit weight of "this is what Korea produces." That origin story is a core part of the brand.

Can K-pop continue to be sold as an authentically Korean cultural export if Korean audiences are tuning out? The $301.7 million in album exports is an impressive figure. But if it's being built on top of domestic disengagement, the foundation deserves scrutiny.

The agencies aren't wrong to follow the money. Markets exist to be served. But the moment K-pop loses its identity as Korean music — not just music that happens to come from Korea — the meaning that global fans attach to it may shift in ways that are difficult to predict or reverse. Right now, K-pop is running an experiment: how far can you grow without your roots? The answer isn't in yet.
